title: A condition map shows where a model was trained against where it is asked to work, and colour adds a third quantity to the grid
summary: Two 3D point clouds fill the same temperature, pressure and equivalence-ratio box. One marks which conditions ignite within a time bound, the other how stiff the chemistry is. A small cluster of circles marks the conditions a reference model was trained on: the maps show how little of the box that is.

media.alt: A 3D scatter plot with temperature from about 800 to 2800 kelvin on one horizontal axis, equivalence ratio from 0.3 to 6 on the other horizontal axis, and pressure from 0.01 to 100 atmospheres on a logarithmic vertical axis. Thousands of small semi-transparent points coloured from purple to pale yellow by equivalence ratio fill most of the box. A small group of black-outlined circles sits low on the left, a tiny part of the volume.

source.caption: Ignitability map (3D)
source.note: Group explainer. Both maps share the same grid; the training-region marker is an external reference's region (legend text), not the author's.
group: 01_02b_ignitability_3d_map: Ignitability map (3D), ignitable points coloured by equivalence ratio (representative)
02_02c_stiffness_3d_map: Stiffness map across conditions, colour = log10 of the Jacobian stiffness ratio

read_the_figure.question: Over which temperature, pressure and mixture conditions does the chemistry ignite and how hard is it to integrate, compared with the region a reference model was trained on?
read_the_figure.axes: x: temperature T in K (ticks 1000 to 2500). Depth axis: equivalence ratio phi from 0.3 to 6.0 in steps of 0.3 (title). z: pressure in atm on a log scale from 0.01 to 100. Each point is one condition. Map 1: colour = phi, points only where the mixture ignites within the 10 s bound (title). Map 2: colour = log10 of the Jacobian stiffness ratio, from 10 to 15 on the colour bar. Black circles: the reference model's 30 training conditions (legend: phi = 0.5:0.2:1.5, P = 1 atm).
look_at: Find the circles: a small block on the left at about 1 atm. Everything else in the box is outside the training region.
Map 1: the cloud does not fill the whole box. The empty parts are conditions that do not ignite within 10 s; its edge is the ignition boundary.
Map 2: the colour varies smoothly with pressure and temperature, from blue (low stiffness, about 10 to 11) to red (high, about 14 to 15). Look for where the training circles sit on that colour scale.
Colour in map 1 repeats the equivalence-ratio axis. It adds depth cues but no new information.
read_the_figure.proves: That the sweep covers a very large volume of conditions of which the training set is a tiny corner, and that stiffness varies by several orders of magnitude over it. It does not by itself show how a model performs away from the training region.
if_wrong: A 3D scatter hides points behind others: a fixed viewpoint can make a region look empty or full. Rotate, or use slices.
A colour bar from 10 to 15 on a log10 scale is a range of five orders of magnitude, much larger than the colour change suggests.
Semi-transparent points make dense regions look uniform: counts are lost.
must_check: All three axes labelled with units, with log scales marked (pressure here).
Colour bar labelled with its quantity and whether it is logarithmic: yes (log10 of the stiffness ratio).
The ignition criterion is stated: here a 10 s time bound; the definition of ignition (for example a temperature rise) is not on the figure.
The training region is drawn in the same coordinates as the grid: yes, as circles.
Slices or marginal projections are offered, since a 3D view hides structure.
as_drawn: Grid: phi has 20 values (0.3 to 6.0 in steps of 0.3, computed). The numbers of temperature and pressure grid points are not stated.
Training region: phi = 0.5:0.2:1.5 gives 6 values (0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.1, 1.3, 1.5); with 30 conditions that leaves 5 values of another variable, not stated on the figure.
Stiffness colour bar: 10 to 15 in log10, so the stiffness ratio runs from about 1e10 to 1e15 over the map (as printed on the colour bar).

terms.meaning: The fuel-to-oxidiser ratio divided by its stoichiometric value. Below 1 is lean, 1 is stoichiometric, above 1 is rich.
A condition at which the mixture ignites within the chosen time bound. Here 10 s; the figure does not define ignition itself.
The ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue magnitude of the chemical Jacobian. It measures the spread of time scales in the system.
A system is stiff when fast and slow processes coexist, so explicit solvers must take tiny steps for stability even when the solution is smooth.
The set of inputs a data-driven model was fitted on. Predictions outside it are extrapolations.
How well a set of sample points fills the input space. Dense grids give coverage; a small cluster does not.
An axis or colour bar where equal steps are equal ratios. Pressure here spans four decades.

remember: Equivalence ratio phi = (F/O) / (F/O)_stoich; phi = 1 is the balanced mixture.
Stiffness ratio S = |lambda_max| / |lambda_min|: the ratio of the fastest to the slowest rate.
A colour bar in log10 hides that equal colour steps are factors of ten.
A 3D scatter has a viewpoint: check for hidden points.
Training coverage is not performance: it only says where the model has seen data.

understand.title: Why map ignition at all
understand.text: Before testing a model you must know where there is something to predict. Conditions that never ignite within the bound have no ignition delay; the ignitability map draws that boundary.

understand.title: Why map stiffness
understand.text: Stiffness tells you how hard the problem is to integrate and how many time scales a data-driven model must capture. A map across conditions shows where the numerical difficulty grows.

understand.title: Why overlay the training region
understand.text: The circles turn the map into an argument about extrapolation. The wide coloured cloud is where the model might be asked to work; the circles are where it has data. The figure is a coverage argument, not a performance result.

steps.title: Equivalence ratio
steps.note: For hydrogen and oxygen, 2 H2 + O2 gives water, so the stoichiometric fuel-to-oxygen mole ratio is 2 and phi = 1 at H2 : O2 = 2 : 1.

steps.title: Stiffness ratio
steps.note: The eigenvalues of the Jacobian of the chemical source terms are rates. The figure plots the base-10 logarithm of this ratio.

steps.title: Why it costs steps
steps.note: Explicit Euler is stable only for steps below 2 over the fastest rate. If the slow time scale is 1 / |lambda_min|, a run over a few of those slow times needs a number of steps proportional to S.

steps.title: Implicit methods remove the step limit
steps.note: An implicit step solves an equation at each step but is stable for any step size on a decaying mode, so the step is chosen for accuracy, not stability.

steps.title: Log colour
steps.note: A colour value of 13 means a stiffness ratio of 1e13. Moving from 10 to 15 on the colour bar changes S by a factor of 100,000.

steps.title: Counting the grid
steps.note: The grid is the product of the three axis counts. Only phi is fully specified in the title: 20 values.

steps.title: Training points as a fraction of the grid
steps.note: With any grid of reasonable resolution (hundreds of values per plane) the training set is a fraction of a percent of the points, which is what the small cluster of circles shows.

worked.title: How many phi values and training conditions?
worked.problem: The title gives phi from 0.3 to 6.0 in steps of 0.3, and the training legend gives phi = 0.5:0.2:1.5 with 30 conditions. How many phi values does each have, and how many other values does the training set contain?

solution.text: Sweep: number of steps plus one.
Training: the same count for the range 0.5 to 1.5 in steps of 0.2.

worked.answer: 20 values in the sweep, 6 in the training set, so each phi has 5 conditions of the third variable (not stated on the figure).

analyze.q: The ignitable cloud has a visible edge. What physical variable do you expect the boundary to depend on most, and how would you test it with a slice?
analyze.hint: Think of ignition delay against temperature at fixed pressure and phi.

analyze.q: In the stiffness map find the colours at the training circles. Is the training region typical of the whole map or an extreme of it?
analyze.hint: Compare the circles' colour with the range in the cloud.

analyze.q: Why is colour in map 1 redundant, and what could it show instead?
analyze.hint: It repeats the phi axis; use colour for ignition delay.

evaluate.q: Does this pair of figures show that the reference model fails away from the training region? State what additional figure would.
evaluate.hint: A prediction error map over the same grid.

evaluate.q: Improve the figure for a reader who cannot rotate it: choose two or three slices and say why.
evaluate.hint: Fixed pressure, fixed phi, fixed temperature.

create: Design a coverage map that colours each grid point by distance to the nearest training condition, and describe how that would sharpen the extrapolation claim.
Sketch the ignitability map as a set of three 2D panels at three pressures.

checks.answer: The ratio of the fastest to the slowest rate of the linearised system: |lambda_max| / |lambda_min| of the Jacobian.

checks.q: A colour value of 12.5 on the stiffness colour bar corresponds to what stiffness ratio?
checks.hint: 10 to the power of the value.

checks.q: Why do stiff problems need implicit solvers?
checks.hint: Stability limit of the explicit step.
checks.answer: An explicit solver needs a step below about 2 over the fastest rate, regardless of how smooth the solution is, so the number of steps grows in proportion to the stiffness. An implicit solver has no such limit on a decaying mode.

checks.q: Is it fair to conclude that a model trained on the circles is unreliable on the whole cloud?
checks.answer: No. The figure shows coverage, not performance. It makes extrapolation a risk; a prediction-error map would test it.

checks.q: How would you quantify how much of the grid lies near the training set?
checks.answer: Compute, for every grid point, the normalised distance to the nearest training condition and report the fraction of points below a chosen distance.
